questions.stem: Why did ancient Greece develop as many independent city-states rather than as one kingdom?
options: The Persian king had forbidden the Greek cities to unite
Great rivers flooded every year and cut the cities off from each other
Mountains and sea divided communities, so each grew separately
Each city spoke its own language that the others could not understand
questions.explanation: Greece is a land of rugged mountains, narrow valleys and many islands, which made overland travel difficult and encouraged each community to govern itself. All Greeks spoke dialects of the same language and shared gods and festivals such as the Olympic Games, even though they rarely united politically. Greece has no great flooding rivers like the Nile.

questions.stem: What was a polis in ancient Greece?
options: An open market place where citizens met to trade and talk
A meeting of all the citizens of a city to vote on its new laws
A city-state: a city and its farmland, with its own government
A fortified hill at the centre of a city, holding its temples
questions.explanation: A polis, such as Athens or Sparta, was an independent state made up of a city and the countryside around it, with its own laws, army and patron gods. The fortified hill is the acropolis, the market place is the agora, and the citizens' meeting in Athens was the Assembly, or ekklesia.

questions.stem: From about 750 BCE many Greek city-states founded colonies around the Mediterranean and Black Sea. What was a main reason?
options: To escape Roman armies that were conquering mainland Greece
To spread the new religion of Christianity to other peoples
The Persian king paid Greeks to settle on his empire's borders
A shortage of good farmland at home, and the search for trade
questions.explanation: Mountainous Greece had limited farmland for a growing population, so groups set out to found new cities in places such as southern Italy, Sicily, southern France and around the Black Sea, which also became trading partners. Syracuse and Massalia (modern Marseille) began this way. Rome conquered Greece much later, in the 100s BCE, and Christianity began centuries after that.

questions.stem: Which Athenian is usually credited with founding democracy through his reforms of 508/507 BCE?
options: Draco
Themistocles
Cleisthenes
Pericles
questions.explanation: Cleisthenes reorganised Athenian citizens into new tribes, created the Council of 500 and gave power to the Assembly, laying the foundations of democracy. Pericles led Athens later, in the 400s BCE, when its democracy was at its height. Draco wrote Athens' first harsh law code, and Themistocles was the general who built up Athens' navy against Persia.

questions.stem: In Athenian democracy, what was the Assembly (ekklesia)?
options: A council of 500 nobles who held their seats for life
A court of judges appointed by the city's leading general
A meeting where any male citizen could speak and vote on laws
A parliament of representatives elected by citizens every few years
questions.explanation: Athens was a direct democracy: citizens themselves debated and voted in the Assembly on laws, war and peace, often with thousands attending on the Pnyx hill. Australia is a representative democracy, where voters elect members of parliament to decide for them. The Council of 500 was chosen by lot each year to prepare business for the Assembly, not appointed for life.

questions.stem: Which group could take part in the Athenian Assembly?
options: Adult men whose parents were Athenian citizens
Wealthy metics who had lived in Athens for years
Women from the leading citizen families
Educated slaves who could read and write
questions.explanation: Only adult male citizens could vote, and after a law of 451 BCE a citizen needed both parents to be Athenian. Metics (resident foreigners), women and slaves were all excluded, so only a minority of the people living in Athens had a political say. This is an important limit on calling Athens a democracy in the modern sense.

questions.stem: What was ostracism in ancient Athens?
options: A fine for citizens who failed to turn up and vote
A vote to send a citizen into exile for ten years
A trial that ended in death by drinking poison
A lifelong ban on speaking in the Assembly
questions.explanation: Citizens scratched a name on a piece of broken pottery called an ostrakon, and the man with the most votes, if enough were cast, had to leave Athens for ten years. It was meant to stop any one man becoming too powerful. Death by poison was the sentence carried out on Socrates after a trial, which is a different process.

questions.stem: In Sparta, who were the helots?
options: Officials elected each year to watch over the two kings
Enslaved people owned by the state who farmed the Spartans' land
Free non-citizens who worked as traders and craftsmen
Spartan boys in their years of military training
questions.explanation: Helots were the conquered peoples of Laconia and Messenia, forced to farm the land and hand over much of the harvest so that Spartan citizens (Spartiates) could train full time as soldiers. The free non-citizens who traded and made goods were the perioikoi. Fear of a helot revolt shaped Spartan life and helps explain its strict military discipline.

questions.stem: What happened to Spartan boys at about the age of seven?
options: They started school in the city to study philosophy and public speaking
They were apprenticed to a craftsman to learn a useful trade
They were sent to Athens to be educated by its best teachers
They left home to begin tough military training in the agoge
questions.explanation: In the agoge, Spartan boys lived in groups, endured hunger and hardship and trained to become hoplites loyal to the state. Studying philosophy and public speaking was more typical of wealthy Athenian boys. Trades and crafts in Sparta were left to the perioikoi.

questions.stem: Compared with women in Athens, women in Sparta:
options: could vote in the Spartan assembly alongside the male citizens
fought as hoplites in the phalanx beside the men whenever the city was at war
were kept indoors and were not allowed to exercise in public
could own land and had more freedom to move about outside the home
questions.explanation: Spartan women ran households and estates while men trained and fought, could own and inherit land, and exercised so that they would bear strong children. Athenian citizen women, in contrast, were expected to stay mostly indoors. Women in neither city could vote or fight as hoplites.

questions.stem: Greek hoplites fought in a phalanx. What was a phalanx?
options: A tall wooden siege tower that was rolled up against an enemy's walls
A tight block of soldiers with overlapping shields and spears
A warship powered by three rows of oarsmen on each side
A charge by cavalry led from the front by the city's king
questions.explanation: Hoplites were citizen soldiers with a large round shield, spear and armour; in the phalanx each man's shield partly protected the man beside him, so the formation worked only if everyone held their place. The warship with three banks of oars was the trireme, which gave Athens its naval power.

questions.stem: In 490 BCE an Athenian army defeated a Persian invasion force at the Battle of:
options: Salamis
Plataea
Marathon
Thermopylae
questions.explanation: At Marathon the Athenians and their Plataean allies defeated the first Persian invasion, sent by Darius I. Thermopylae and the sea battle of Salamis came ten years later, in 480 BCE, during Xerxes' invasion, and the land battle of Plataea in 479 BCE ended it. The modern marathon race takes its name from the legend of a runner carrying news of the victory.

questions.stem: Why is the Battle of Thermopylae (480 BCE) remembered, even though the Greeks lost?
options: Alexander the Great won his first major victory over the Persians there
Leonidas and a small force held a narrow pass against a huge Persian army
It was the final battle of the long Peloponnesian War between Sparta and Athens
The Athenian navy destroyed the Persian fleet in the narrow straits there
questions.explanation: King Leonidas of Sparta, with his 300 Spartans and several thousand other Greeks, held the pass for days until a local man showed the Persians a path around it; Leonidas and his rearguard fought to the death. Their stand became a lasting symbol of courage and sacrifice. The Persian fleet was defeated soon afterwards at Salamis, not at Thermopylae.

questions.stem: Why was the Battle of Salamis (480 BCE) a turning point in the Persian Wars?
options: Alexander the Great defeated King Darius III there
The Greek fleet beat the larger Persian navy in narrow waters
Spartan hoplites captured the Persian king Xerxes in battle
Athens surrendered and became part of the Persian Empire
questions.explanation: Themistocles lured the Persian fleet into the narrow strait between Salamis and the mainland, where its greater numbers were a disadvantage, and the Greek triremes won a decisive victory. Without control of the sea Xerxes could not easily supply his huge army, and he took much of it back to Asia. The Persians had burned Athens shortly before, but Athens never surrendered.

questions.stem: The historian Thucydides argued that the main underlying cause of the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BCE) was:
options: Philip of Macedon's march with his army into southern Greece
the growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta
a Persian invasion that Sparta refused to help Athens fight off
Rome's attempt to conquer Greece and add it to its own empire
questions.explanation: Thucydides, who lived through the war, separated the immediate quarrels, such as disputes over Corcyra and Potidaea, from the deeper cause: Athens' growing empire through the Delian League alarmed Sparta and its allies. Sparta eventually won in 404 BCE, helped by Persian money for its fleet. Philip of Macedon conquered Greece later, in 338 BCE.

questions.stem: Why did Greeks travel to the sanctuary at Delphi?
options: To worship Athena in the Parthenon, her greatest temple
To ask the god Apollo for advice through his priestess, the Pythia
To compete in the Olympic Games, which were held there every four years
To vote in the Assembly that governed all the Greek cities
questions.explanation: At Delphi the Pythia, Apollo's priestess, gave often puzzling answers to questions from cities and individuals, for example about founding colonies or going to war. The Olympic Games were held at Olympia, a different sanctuary honouring Zeus, and the Parthenon, temple of Athens' patron goddess Athena, is in Athens. No single assembly ruled all the Greek cities.

questions.stem: In Greek myth, why did Zeus punish Prometheus?
options: He started the Trojan War by stealing Helen of Sparta
He killed the monster Medusa without Zeus's permission
He stole fire from the gods and gave it to humans
He opened a jar that let evils loose into the world
questions.explanation: Prometheus took fire from the gods and gave it to people, and Zeus punished him by chaining him to a rock where an eagle ate his liver every day. Opening the jar of evils is the story of Pandora, the Trojan War began when Paris took Helen, and Medusa was killed by Perseus. Myths like these explained the world and the relationship between gods and humans.

questions.stem: Homer's Iliad tells part of the story of:
options: Aeneas fleeing from Troy to found a new home in Italy
the Trojan War, focusing on the anger of the hero Achilles
Odysseus' ten-year voyage home to Ithaca after the war
the Persian invasion of Greece and the stand at Thermopylae
questions.explanation: The Iliad covers a few weeks in the tenth year of the siege of Troy and centres on Achilles, the greatest Greek warrior, whose pursuit of glory and honour showed Greek heroic ideals. Odysseus' journey home is told in Homer's other epic, the Odyssey, and Aeneas' journey is the subject of Virgil's Roman epic, the Aeneid.

questions.stem: What was one lasting effect of Alexander the Great's conquests?
options: His single empire stayed united for more than 300 years
Latin became the common language of the eastern Mediterranean
Persia conquered Greece and ruled it for several centuries
Greek language and culture spread across Egypt and western Asia
questions.explanation: Alexander's conquests, from Egypt to north-western India, began the Hellenistic age, in which Greek became the shared language of trade and learning and Greek-style cities such as Alexandria in Egypt flourished. His empire split among his generals soon after his death in 323 BCE. Latin spread in the west with Rome, while Greek remained dominant in the east.

questions.stem: Which Athenian philosopher was sentenced to death in 399 BCE for 'corrupting the youth' and disrespecting the gods?
options: Aristotle
Pythagoras
Socrates
Plato
questions.explanation: Socrates taught by asking probing questions, and he was condemned by an Athenian jury and died by drinking hemlock. His student Plato recorded his ideas and founded the Academy, and Plato's student Aristotle later became tutor to Alexander the Great. Socrates himself wrote nothing down.

questions.stem: Why is Hippocrates often called the 'father of medicine'?
options: He built the first public hospital in the city of ancient Rome
He taught that illness had natural causes, not punishment from gods
He discovered that germs carried by tiny organisms cause disease
He performed the first successful surgery using an anaesthetic
questions.explanation: Hippocrates and his followers observed patients carefully, recorded symptoms and looked for natural causes and treatments, and the Hippocratic Oath for doctors still carries his name. Germ theory was developed in the 1800s by scientists such as Louis Pasteur, more than 2,000 years later. Hippocrates lived on the Greek island of Kos, not in Rome.

questions.stem: Which order of Greek column is the plainest, with a simple cushion-shaped top, as used on the Parthenon?
options: Corinthian
Composite
Doric
Ionic
questions.explanation: Doric columns are sturdy, with no base and a plain capital, as on the Parthenon. Ionic columns have scroll-shaped volutes at the top, and Corinthian columns are decorated with carved acanthus leaves. Composite is a later Roman style combining the two, and all of these styles still appear on parliament houses, banks and museums today.

questions.stem: The word 'draconian', meaning extremely harsh, comes from Draco of Athens. What did Draco do?
options: Ruled Sparta as a cruel king who enslaved the helots
Led the Persian army that burned Athens in 480 BCE
Ordered the execution of Socrates for questioning the gods
Wrote Athens' first written law code, with death for many crimes
questions.explanation: Around 621 BCE Draco wrote down Athens' laws for the first time, so they were no longer known only to the aristocrats who judged cases, but the punishments were so harsh that even small thefts could bring death. Later writers said his laws were written in blood. Solon replaced most of them about a generation later.
